lesson.grammar_point: participle clauses (reduced relative and adverbial clauses)

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: something small that carries you to the next stage
the one thing you keep failing to notice about yourself
a point that marks real progress on a long road
gained only after a great deal of effort
to start to make sense and work out well
to stop and look carefully at where you are
to stop improving and stay at the same level
to do the quiet work that makes later success possible

paras: Having ridden in eleven countries over fifteen years, I finally did something I had been putting off: I took stock. Not a photo album, not a list of countries. An honest audit. Laid out on the kitchen table were fifteen notebooks, one for each season, and reading them in order was like listening to a much younger man talk. The first three are all distance and no detail. Written in a hurry at the end of enormous days, they record kilometers and nothing else. The later ones are slower, full of names and weather and food, and that difference, it turns out, is the whole story of how far I have come.

The audit was not flattering. Comparing the notebooks year by year, I could see exactly where I had plateaued: somewhere around year eight, having learned enough to be comfortable, I quietly stopped learning anything at all. There was also a blind spot I had never admitted to. Every trip that fell through, fell through for the same reason. I had planned the riding and ignored the resting. The trips that worked were the ones with a rest day built in, which is the hard-won lesson of a man who took a decade to notice the obvious. Milestones are easy. They count themselves. Blind spots have to be hunted.

So the next one is being built differently. Sitting with the map last week, I stopped drawing lines between cities and started marking the days I will not ride at all. The route, sketched in pencil and left deliberately loose after the first week, now has three rest days in it and a ferry I have not booked. None of this is new knowledge. It is old knowledge finally falling into place. Fifteen years, eleven countries and a shelf of notebooks are not a destination. They are a stepping stone, the groundwork quietly laid, for whatever the next fifteen turn out to be.

gapfill.text: This text runs on PARTICIPLE CLAUSES. They let you put two ideas in one sentence, with no 'and', no 'because', no 'which'. -ING = at the same time, or the reason: 'SITTING with the map, I marked the rest days.' HAVING + past participle = finished BEFORE the main verb: 'HAVING RIDDEN all day, I could barely speak.' PAST PARTICIPLE alone = passive, something was done to it: 'WRITTEN in a hurry, the notes say almost nothing.' And the same shapes shorten a relative clause: 'the notebook LYING on the desk', 'a route SKETCHED in pencil'.

bank.label: Useful language for taking stock
items: Having ridden in eleven countries, I plan very differently now.
Sitting with the map last night, I marked three rest days.
Comparing the notebooks year by year, I could see the pattern.
Written in a hurry, the early notes say almost nothing.
The route, sketched in pencil, is still deliberately loose.
Knowing that road, I would leave an extra day for it.
Having learned that lesson twice, I now build in the rest.
It is groundwork, hard-won and quietly laid.

lf.title: Which one? (blue = it was FINISHED before the main verb)
items: A
Having paid the deposit
, I stopped worrying about the dates.
strong
B
Riding into Porto
, I realized I had never seen the sea from that road.
C
Having lost the map
, we asked at the bakery.
strong
D
The notebook,
written in a hurry
, says almost nothing.

lf.text: A and C, in blue, use HAVING + past participle: the action was finished before the main verb. B is a plain -ing clause: it happens at the SAME time. D has no -ing at all, because a past participle clause is PASSIVE, and somebody else wrote the notebook. So ask yourself first: before, at the same time, or done to it?

items: Scenario 1
Take stock of your riding out loud. Start three sentences with 'Having ...' and say what fifteen years have taught you.
Scenario 2
Describe last week using -ing clauses: 'Sitting with the map, I ...', 'Looking at the route, I ...'.
Scenario 3
Name your blind spot. Say what it is, how long you had it, and what falls apart because of it.
Scenario 4
Describe the next trip in three sentences, each with a reduced clause: a route sketched in pencil, days left open, a ferry not yet booked.

answerkey.title: Reveal the answer key
list: Gap-fill: 1 = Having ridden, 2 = Written, 3 = Comparing, 4 = Having learned, 5 = with a rest day built in, 6 = sketched in pencil.
Model (same time): 'Sitting with the map, I marked three rest days.'
Model (finished before): 'Having ridden in eleven countries, I plan very differently now.'
Model (passive): 'Written in a hurry, the early notes say almost nothing.'
Shapes: -ing = same time or reason. Having + past participle = earlier. Past participle alone = passive.
answerkey.note: One rule decides everything: the participle clause and the main clause must share the SAME subject. 'Having ridden all day, the hotel was a relief' is wrong, because the hotel did not ride. Say 'Having ridden all day, I found the hotel a relief'.

listenings.text: Marcelo, it is Marit. I have been thinking about what you said, about taking stock, and I did the same thing on Sunday. Twenty-two years of riding, laid out on the living room floor in maps and receipts, and honestly it was uncomfortable. Two things came out of it. The first is that I have come a long way, and I never say that out loud. My first tour was four days long and I cried on the second one. The second is my blind spot, and it is not rest, it is money. I have never once written down what a trip actually costs, so every single year I am surprised, and twice a trip has fallen through in March because of it. So this time I am doing it differently. Having made that mistake twice, I am putting a real number on the next ride before I book anything at all. Nothing dramatic. Just consolidating what I already know instead of chasing something new. Send me your route when it falls into place. Talk on Sunday.

Welcome back to the show. Today, the twenty-year question. How do you know whether you are actually getting better? Here is the uncomfortable answer. Most of us stop improving long before we stop practicing. Having reached the level where everything feels comfortable, we quietly stop learning, and then we call that experience. So here is what the people who keep improving do differently. First, they take stock on paper. Not in their heads, on paper, because memory is generous and paper is not. Second, they hunt for the blind spot rather than counting the milestones. Milestones are easy. They count themselves. A blind spot has to be looked for, and it is almost always the boring thing you have been avoiding for years. Third, they consolidate before they expand. Written into every good plan is one season that adds nothing new and simply makes the old things solid. And finally, they treat what they already have as a stepping stone rather than a summit. Twenty trips, twenty years, twenty of anything is not a finish line. It is groundwork, hard-won and quietly laid, for whatever you decide to do next.

extra_audio.text: First, Marcelo takes stock and lays fifteen notebooks out on the kitchen table. Then, comparing them year by year, he sees exactly where he had plateaued. After that, he finds the blind spot he had never admitted: he had planned the riding and ignored the resting. Next, having accepted that hard-won lesson, he sketches the new route in pencil and marks three rest days on it. Finally, the whole plan falls into place, and he treats twenty years on the road as a stepping stone rather than a finish line.
